messiah.title: Sharing Jesus with a Jewish friend
messiah.intro: The hardest conversation on this site, and the one that most demands humility. Not a campaign and not a technique. A friendship in which a real history is named honestly and a real question is eventually asked.
messiah.html:
Name the history first
You, unprompted

"Before I say anything about Jesus, I want to name what Christians have done to Jewish people. The Crusades, the blood libels, the expulsions, the Shoah. That was ours."

Say it before you are asked. Say it without adding a defence of the church.

The list is long and it is not ancient history. Forced disputations. Expulsion from England, France and Spain. Luther in his old age. Pogroms across eastern Europe. Then Europe in the 1940s, in countries that had been Christian for a thousand years.

Nearly every Jewish person has met Christians who deflect this. Being the one who does not is not a technique. It is the price of admission, and it is simply true.

Whatever you say about Jesus will be heard through that history. You do not get to skip it, and you do not get to be wounded that it is there.

Do not rush the sentence either. Let it sit. If your friend says nothing for a while, that is the right response and not a failure.

It also matters that you know the specifics. Vague regret sounds like a script. Naming a year, a decree or a town sounds like someone who went and looked.

Two habits to drop before you start
You, plainly

"I am not asking you to stop being Jewish. I believe Yeshua is the Messiah of Israel, and I would love to talk about that with you sometime."

The first habit is a single word. Never use the word convert at a Jewish person. It belongs to the disputation, the forced sermon and the baptism at sword point. Say what you actually mean instead.

The second habit you may not notice you have. Do not explain the Hebrew Bible to a Jewish friend. It is their book. Many have read it in a language you cannot read, with commentators you have never opened.

Ask how they read a passage. Do not tell them what it means. That one change alters the whole temperature of the conversation.

A third habit is worth dropping too. Stop treating the first Christians as a new religion that arrived from outside.

The first generation of people who followed Yeshua were Jewish. They argued from the Tanakh in synagogues and kept the feasts.

The invitation to work toward
You, in time

"Would you read Isaiah 53 with me, and show me how the Targum and Sukkah 52a read it? I would rather hear it from your sources than mine."

The whole posture sits in that sentence. Their library. Their reading first. You asking rather than telling.

This is the one section of the site where you should expect to learn more than you teach. That is not false modesty. Counter-missionary replies are serious, old and well prepared.

Take one text at a time. Stacking prophecies feels strong and lands as a sales pitch.

Read the counter-missionary answer before you need it. Meeting a good one cold, in a kitchen, is not the moment to hear it for the first time.

4Q521 is worth knowing early. It is a Dead Sea Scroll, older than the church, and it describes a Messiah who heals the blind and raises the dead.

Nobody can call that a Christian invention. That is the kind of source this section is built on.

What actually reaches a Jewish friend
1

Naming the history before you are asked

Say it first and unprompted, every time. Do not wait to be challenged into it. A Jewish friend who hears a Christian name it without being pushed is hearing something rare.

2

Arguing from their sources, not yours

The Targum on Isaiah 53. Sukkah 52a on the two Messiahs. Yoma 39b on the forty years. 4Q521 from the Dead Sea Scrolls. Every one of these is Jewish. Most are rabbinic or older than the church. None can be waved off as a Christian gloss.

3

One text at a time, with real listening

Take one passage. Ask how they read it. Then actually weigh the answer. A Christian who engages the strongest form of a reply is rarer than one who has memorised twelve verses.

4

Friendship measured in years

There is no fast version of this. Pressure reads as the coercion their ancestors lived through. The realistic aim of any single conversation is that they would be willing to have another one.

The method

Say Tanakh, not Old Testament

Old implies replaced, and supersession is the theology behind the history. Small words carry weight here. Tanakh. Yeshua, if it comes naturally. The Hebrew Scriptures. They signal that you know whose book you are holding.

Concede what is genuinely contested

Isaiah 7:14 is weaker than most Christians are taught. Psalm 22:16 has a real textual question. The seventy weeks of Daniel have several defensible arithmetics. Say so before anyone pushes you. That is what buys credit for Isaiah 53, for the terminus in Daniel and for Yoma 39b.

Let Romans 11 set your posture

It is not a courtesy. It is a command. God has not cast away his people. The Gentile branch is grafted in and told plainly not to boast against the root. A Christian who holds that verse cannot patronise a Jewish friend.

Never say the Jews killed Jesus

The deicide charge is the engine behind a thousand years of massacre. It is also bad theology. A Roman prefect ordered the execution, and the New Testament puts the responsibility on all of us. If that phrase is in your vocabulary, take it out for good.

Never quote-mine the Talmud

Most viral Talmud quotations are invented, mistranslated, or stripped of a context that reverses them. They come straight down from medieval disputation propaganda. If you cannot read the passage in context on Sefaria, do not use it.

Not the works-righteousness caricature

Second Temple Judaism was a covenant religion with obligations. It was not a merit ledger. Saying otherwise tells your friend you have never asked them what they believe. So ask. You will learn something, and you will be trusted with the answer.

The part that takes years
You, later

"You are not a project to me. If you never agree with me about this, we are still going to be friends in twenty years."

Mean it, because they will test it. Pressure here does not read as urgency. It reads as the thing their grandparents fled.

There is also a cost you should understand before you speak. For many Jewish families, a child who follows Yeshua is felt as a loss to the family and to the people. That is not stubbornness. It is grief, earned by history.

So go slowly and stay. The aim of any one conversation is only that another one would be welcome.

Ask about their family, their festivals and what they actually keep. Most Christians never do, and the asking is not a strategy. It is friendship.

Romans 11 is the check on all of this. The branch grafted in is warned in the same breath not to boast against the root.

Read that verse often enough and the tone looks after itself.

One more thing is worth saying out loud at some point. You are not asking anyone to leave their people.

Say that you know what it would cost, and that you would not think less of them for never agreeing with you.

Then drop it and talk about something else. The mark of a friendship is that it has other subjects.

If a conversation ever ends badly, go back and apologise for the tone rather than the content. It is almost always the tone that did the damage.

None of this is a method for producing a result. It is how you behave when you believe something and you also love the person you are talking to.

If that sounds slow, it is. It is also the only version of this that has ever been worth anything.

How it actually goes

Targum Jonathan opens Isaiah 52:13 like this. Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper.

— an ancient Jewish rendering, read aloud in synagogues, long before there was an argument to win

The five questions that do the most work

  1. "How do you read Sukkah 52a on the two Messiahs?" The two-Messiah teaching already concedes the two portraits, the suffering one and the reigning one. You are not disputing their tradition. You are asking why one figure coming twice is harder to believe than two figures coming once.
  2. "Daniel says an anointed one is cut off before the sanctuary is destroyed. Who was that?" The sequence has a terminus and the terminus has passed. Skip the arithmetic of the weeks, which can be argued several ways. The order of the events is the whole argument.
  3. "Leviticus 17:11 grounds atonement in blood on an altar. What grounds it now?" Ask it once, gently, and then stop. Judaism has had to answer that for nineteen centuries without the altar the verse names. Yoma 39b records forty years of failed signs before the temple fell.
  4. "Who is the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 made with?" Israel and Judah, by name. The phrase is not a Christian import. It is the promise of a Jewish prophet, and it dissolves the idea that you invented a new religion before that idea can form.
  5. "What would the Messiah have to be for you to look again?" Ask it because you want the answer. It also invites the same question back at you, which is fair, and answering it honestly is worth more than any verse you could produce.

Start here

The servant path walks Isaiah 53 through the Targum and the Talmud. It is the one argument built entirely from their own library. Every case page ends with a suggested question and a scripted back-and-forth, with the counter-missionary reply included.
